t: Longest Palindrome After Substring Concatenation II
o:
## Understanding the problem

We may take any substring `A` of `s` (possibly empty) and any substring `B` of `t` (possibly empty), form `A + B`, and want the longest result that is a palindrome.

**Example 1:** taking "a" from both gives "aa" → answer 2.
**Example 2:** every character differs across the strings, so only single characters work → answer 1.
**Example 3:** the whole of `t` ("aaaa") is already a palindrome longer than anything involving `s` → answer 4.
**Example 4:** taking "abc" from `s` and "ba" from `t` yields "abcba" → answer 5. Note how the palindrome's outer layers come from mirrored parts of the two strings, while the middle can be a palindrome lying entirely inside one of them.

With lengths up to 1000, an $O(n \cdot m)$ dynamic program over character pairs is expected; anything like $O(n^2 m^2)$ enumeration will time out.
k: Any palindrome built as s-substring + t-substring decomposes into matched outer layers (s-suffix vs t-prefix mirrors) plus a middle palindrome fully inside one string.
The mirror-match length f(i, j) = longest k with s[i..i+k-1] == reverse(t[j-k+1..j]) satisfies a simple LCS-like recurrence f(i,j) = f(i+1,j-1)+1 when s[i]==t[j].
Precomputing, for each index, the longest palindrome starting there in s and ending there in t lets every cross candidate be closed out in O(1).

a.i: Enumerate every substring of `s` and every substring of `t`, concatenate them, and test whether the result is a palindrome, keeping the maximum length. This directly models the problem statement and is trivially correct, but with four nested index choices plus an $O(n+m)$ palindrome check it is far too slow for $n, m = 1000$; it serves as the conceptual baseline.
s: Collect all substrings of s and all substrings of t (or just their index ranges).
For every pair of ranges, conceptually concatenate them.
Check whether the concatenation is a palindrome with a two-pointer scan.
Track and return the maximum length seen.
a.t: O(n^2 · m^2 · (n+m)) — four nested range choices times a linear palindrome check; hopeless at n = m = 1000.
a.sp: O(n + m) for temporary substring storage.

a.n: Approach 2: Mirror-Match DP + Per-Index Best Palindromes
a.i: Any palindrome $P = A + B$ (with $A$ a suffix-piece of `s` and $B$ a prefix-piece of `t`) has layered structure: its first $k$ characters mirror its last $k$, so $s[i..i+k-1]$ must equal the reverse of $t[j-k+1..j]$, and the untouched middle must itself be a palindrome starting at $i+k$ in `s` or ending at $j-k$ in `t`. Define $f(i,j)$ = largest such $k$; it obeys $f(i,j)=f(i{+}1,j{-}1)+1$ when $s[i]=t[j]$, else 0 — computed in one $O(nm)$ table. Separately compute $\text{suf}[i]$ = longest palindromic substring of `s` starting at $i$, and $\text{pre}[j]$ = longest palindromic substring of `t` ending at $j$ (via the classic interval palindrome DP). Then the answer is the best single-string palindrome, or $2f(i,j) + \max(\text{suf}[i{+}f],\ \text{pre}[j{-}f{+}1])$ over all pairs.
s: Build boolean tables palS / palT with the standard recurrence pal[i][j] = (x[i]==x[j]) && (j-i<2 || pal[i+1][j-1]).
Derive suf[i] = max length palindrome of s starting at i, and pre[j] = max length palindrome of t ending at j.
Fill f(i, j): if s[i]==t[j], f[i][j] = f[i+1][j-1] + 1 (iterate i downward, j upward); otherwise 0.
Initialize ans = max(suf) and max(pre) to cover palindromes inside one string.
For every (i, j) with k = f[i][j] > 0, consider 2k + max(suf[i+k] if in range, pre[j-k+1] if in range); return the overall maximum.
a.t: O(n² + m² + nm) — the palindrome tables are quadratic in each string, and the mirror-match table visits every (i, j) pair once.
a.sp: O(n² + m² + nm) for the three DP tables (the palindrome tables can be reduced to O(n) rolling rows if needed).

## Wrap-up

In an interview, state the brute force briefly to show you understand the structure, then move straight to the mirror-match formulation: the key observation is that a cross palindrome peels into matched outer layers plus an inner palindrome, and both pieces admit clean DPs. Choose Approach 2 as your final answer — it comfortably handles n = m = 1000.

Common pitfalls: forgetting palindromes that lie entirely inside `s` or entirely inside `t` (covered here by initializing with max(suf)/max(pre)); off-by-one errors when indexing `suf[i+k]` versus `pre[j-k]`; and iterating `f` in the wrong direction (it needs `f[i+1][j-1]`, so go bottom-up on `i`). Edge cases include empty selections (answer is always at least 1 since single characters exist), identical strings, and no common characters at all. Likely follow-ups: reducing memory to O(n) with rolling arrays, handling lengths up to 10⁵ with Manacher-based preprocessing, or returning the actual palindrome rather than its length.
